title: Impact of Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger revealed by a single cosmic clock: thick-to-thin disc transition, gas disc shrinking and bar formation
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Whether the formation of the Galactic bar was connected to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) merger, the last significant merger experienced by the Milky Way, remains an open question. The bar formation epoch has been inferred from the star formation history of the nuclear stellar disc (NSD) traced by Mira variables, and the GSE merger epoch from the age-metallicity relation of red giants. However, these epochs rest on different stellar tracers with different age scales and cannot be compared directly. We recalibrate the Mira period-age relation onto the age scale of APOGEE red giants, with ages from a Bayesian neural network trained on Kepler asteroseismic ages. We fit the Gaia DR3 proper motions of 2394 O-rich disc Mira variables with an action-based quasi-isothermal distribution function whose parameters vary with period, and derive the period-age relation by matching their vertical velocity dispersion as a function of period to that of the APOGEE red giants as a function of age in Funakoshi et al. (2025). This places the NSD star-formation rise and peak at 8.5-10.5 Gyr ago on the red giant age scale, overlapping with the final stage of the GSE-induced starburst, thick-to-thin disc transition and the contraction of the star-forming gas disc. If NSD star formation traces bar formation, these coincidences suggest a possible scenario in which the GSE seeded the bar formation, while fresh gas supplied by the GSE and outer disc gas driven inward by its tidal torques, increased the baryonic dominance of the inner Galaxy.

title: The THESAN-ZOOM project: the delayed rise of Lyman continuum escape fractions in bursty high-redshift galaxies
comment: 26 pages, 24 figures. Comments welcome
summary: The ionizing radiation that galaxies release into their surroundings depends on whether efficient Lyman continuum (LyC) escape coincides with strong photon production. Stellar feedback can open escape paths as the source population fades, linking the escaping radiation to a galaxy's recent history. We investigate this timing in thirteen high-redshift (z > 3) target haloes from the THESAN-ZOOM radiation-hydrodynamic simulations, post-processed with COLT radiative transfer and sampled at ~10 Myr intervals. The clearest delayed relationship links $\text{SFR}_{10}/\text{SFR}_{100}$ to the LyC escape fraction. Selecting the nearest positive cross-correlation peak gives typical lags of ~16 Myr and peak correlations of 0.4-0.6 in massive haloes, with longer and less coherent delays towards lower masses. The fitted delays scale approximately as $M_\star^{-0.19}$ and $M_\text{halo}^{-0.27}$, although the shortest lags approach the native snapshot spacing. Recurrent variations span multiple amplitude-dependent timescales, consistent with repeated episodes of star formation and feedback. Recent star formation closely tracks both intrinsic and escaping photon rates, while the escape fraction reflects the evolving gas transparency. The H$\alpha$-to-UV luminosity ratio retains a delayed association with escape, offering an observable connection between burst phase and leakage. High transparency during a fading phase can nevertheless yield little escaping radiation. The temporal overlap of photon production and transmission therefore shapes both the amount and timing of escaping radiation, informing the interpretation of observed leakers and their contribution to cosmic reionization.

title: The black hole-galaxy correlations of the 12 micron local AGN sample: a NuSTAR perspective
comment: 12 pages, 9 figures (+ Appendix), accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: The M-sigma correlation of inactive galaxies plays a crucial role in estimating the black hole mass (MBH) in active galactic nuclei (AGN): 1) it is used to calibrate the reverberation mapping (RM) method; 2) the RM is the basis of the single epoch method, the most-used technique to determine MBH of broad-line AGN; and 3) in narrow-line AGN, MBH is often directly inferred from the M-sigma correlation. The main goal of this work is to test whether the M-sigma relation calibrated from inactive galaxies can be reliably applied to a local AGN population spanning Seyfert 1, Seyfert 2, and hidden broad-line region galaxies (HBLRs), and whether the resulting AGN relation has sufficient predictive power to be used as an indirect MBH estimator. To investigate this hypothesis, we used the 12 micron AGN sample, a local representative and largely unbiased sample. Since a substantial fraction of this sample has good-quality NuSTAR data, we estimated their MBH with the X-ray scaling method, which works for any AGN accreting at moderate or high level. We find that the M-sigma correlation of the 12 micron AGN sample is different from the one obtained with inactive galaxies and has a substantial scatter. Therefore, its predictive power for MBH estimates is fairly limited. We also find that the MBH-Mgal correlation based on the 12 micron AGN sample is consistent with the analogous correlation obtained from a large sample of nearby type 1 AGN and inconsistent with that of inactive galaxies. Finally, we find suggestive evidence that Seyfert 1 and HBLRs have similar and systematically higher Eddington ratios than Seyfert 2 galaxies.

title: The LBT Y$_{\rm p}$ Project VI: Gas-Phase Chemical Abundance Patterns of Metal-Poor Nebulae
comment: 33 pages, 15 figures, 2 tables, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal. Comments welcome
summary: Through a combined rest-optical and NIR observing campaign, the Large Binocular Telescope Primordial He Abundance ($Y_{\rm p}$) Project has delivered a precision measurement of $Y_{\rm p}$. Given the stringent requirements to measure gas-phase He abundances, the optical spectra contain emission features from a plethora of metals in the Interstellar Medium (ISM). We present gas-phase N, O, Ne, S, Cl, Ar, K and Fe abundance patterns in 62 low-metallicity nebulae. We assess ionization correction factors for each element and select those that reproduce the observed ionic abundance trends. The Ne/O, S/O, and Ar/O abundances do not evolve with metallicity and agree with the solar ratios. Given the Type Ia enrichment of S and Ar, the solar S/O and Ar/O suggest extended star formation histories in local galaxies relative to high-$z$ galaxies at fixed O/H. We report the first ISM K abundances in low-metallicity extragalactic nebulae; both Cl/O and K/O are constant with O/H, indicating the production of these odd-Z elements follows that of $\alpha$ elements. Consistent with prior analyses, gas-phase Fe/O is observed to decrease with O/H due to dust depletion; correcting for this produces an average [Fe/O]$=$$-$0.80, implying Fe-deficient stars capable of producing hard ionizing spectra. Finally, the metallicity-insensitive log(N/O) plateau from 50 nebulae is $-$1.43$\pm$0.10, consistent with previous works. Five galaxies have N/O significantly enhanced relative to the primary plateau, and we discuss their properties, mechanisms that could bias measurements of N/O, and nucleosynthetic progenitors that can produce enhanced N at low metallicity.

title: The PAU Survey: Active galactic nucleus galaxies in galaxy pairs
comment: 16 pages, 18 figures, accepted by A&A
summary: Aims. Leveraging the high-precision photometric redshifts of the Physics of the Accelerating Universe Survey (PAUS), we aim to investigate the connection between active galactic nuclei (AGNs) and galaxy pairs up to redshifts of $\sim1.0$. Methods. We identified 16,824 galaxy pairs with projected separations of $r_p < 100$ kpc and radial-velocity differences of $\Delta V < 3500$ km s$^{-1}$. AGNs were selected by cross-matching PAUS galaxies with multi-wavelength AGN catalogues, yielding 270 AGNs in pairs out of a parent sample of 8,880 AGNs in PAUS. We constructed control samples of isolated AGNs; non-AGNs in pairs; and isolated non-AGNs matched in redshift, absolute magnitude, and environment. Results. Active galactic nuclei in pairs show progressively redder rest-frame colours with increasing redshift, particularly at redshifts of $z\gtrsim 0.5$, whereas isolated AGNs and non-AGNs in pairs show no significant colour evolution and remain at $\mathrm{M_g-M_r}\sim0.65$. Pairs hosting AGNs are also preferentially morphologically disturbed interacting systems found at smaller projected separations and velocity offsets, consistent with more dynamically advanced interactions. Conclusions. These results provide evidence of a redshift-dependent link between galaxy interactions and AGN activity, suggesting that interactions play an increasingly important role in triggering nuclear activity at intermediate redshifts. This study highlights the unique capability of PAUS to probe AGN-galaxy interaction connections beyond the local Universe with unprecedented statistical power.

title: Optical-Infrared Extinction Variation in Nearby Molecular Clouds
summary: The dust extinction curve is an important probe of the properties of dust grains, particularly their size distribution. The properties of dust grains are expected to change significantly in dense molecular clouds due to shielding from interstellar radiation and increased frequency of grain-grain and grain-gas collisions. We measure the dust extinction curve shape parameter R(V) in 9 nearby, dense molecular clouds using data from the APOGEE spectroscopic survey, in combination with ten-band photometry from PS1, 2MASS, and WISE. We analyze the results to determine how the extinction curve varies in nearby molecular clouds. We find that most molecular clouds show a positive correlation between R(V) and E(B-V), but the strength of the correlation varies significantly between clouds. In addition, we find that the clouds with the strongest correlation tend to have very high dispersion in R(V) at fixed E(B-V), which tightens dramatically when clouds are subdivided into separate regions. This suggests that local environmental conditions beyond density shape the R(V)-E(B-V) relation.

title: Optical and near-infrared s-process abundance scales in the Galactic disc
comment: 10 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in A&A
summary: A discrepancy has recently emerged between optical and near-infrared (NIR) s-process abundance scales, particularly for Neodymium (Nd). We investigated this issue using a direct cross-match between the optical Gaia-ESO Survey (DR5) and NIR SDSS-V/MWM (DR19). While atmospheric parameters and Cerium (Ce) abundances exhibit robust 1:1 correlations, Nd displays a systematic X-shaped vertical stretching. Our analysis reveals that the SDSS-V pipeline expands intrinsic Nd variations by a scaling factor of 5.54 relative to the stable optical baseline. This phenomenon is driven by baseline compression in the APOGEE H-band, where the growth of the molecular forest (CN and CO) at high metallicities depresses the local continuum. This forces the chi^2 minimisation engine in the NIR abundance determination to inflate derived abundances to reach mathematical convergence. We provide an empirical calibration framework to reconcile these disparate regimes. This correction effectively eliminates the contradictory negative radial [Nd/Fe] gradient of -0.052 dex/kpc reported in recent NIR surveys, bringing them into alignment with the rising trends established by the optical high-resolution Gaia-ESO survey. These results demonstrate that the observed scale expansion is a spectroscopic artefact of line-blanketing rather than a physical Galactic trend.

title: JWST observations of the planetary nebula NGC 6302 IV: PAH spectral characteristics, formation and evolution
comment: 20 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables including 6 in appendices, accepted in MNRAS
summary: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and carbonaceous dust have been observed in Oxygen-rich planetary nebulae (PNe), yet their formation and evolution in these environments is an open question. We aim to study the formation and evolution of the PAHs in the O-rich PN NGC 6302, by characterizing the PAH emission throughout this object. We obtained JWST MIRI IFU spectroscopic observations of NGC 6302 pointed at its central source. From these, we extract four template spectra that are representative of the variation in PAH emission throughout NGC 6302. We detect the major PAH features at 6.2, 7.7, 8.6, 11.2, and 12.7 $\mu$m, and several minor PAH features. The template spectra vary in terms of their PAH feature widths, peak wavelengths, and relative intensities. The 11.2 $\mu$m PAH feature is class B, typical for PNe. The 6-9 $\mu$m PAH features are class A, which is less common for PNe. We estimate the PAH charge to be 75% cations on average, based on the 7.7/11.2 PAH feature ratio. The relative strengths of the 11-15 $\mu$m PAH features indicate a range of PAH edge structures. To ensure consistency in our observations and explain variable PAH feature widths, we propose a variation in the size of the PAHs throughout NGC 6302, and suggest variation in the shielding of these PAHs. The PAHs range from large and non-compact, to small and compact. We find that NGC 6302 formed PAHs in-situ in the current PN phase, likely from small hydrocarbons formed by the photodissociation of CO.

title: A Potential New Dimension of Astrophysical Aromatic Functionalization: Phosphaethynyl (CP) Derivatives
summary: Quantum chemical computations outline a thermodynamically viable, low-temperature, gas-phase formation pathway for phosphaethynyl cyclopropenylidene ($c$-C$_3$HCP), resulting from cyclopropenylidene ($c$-C$_3$H$_2$) and the phosphaethynyl (CP) radical. Given the detections of both $c$-C$_3$H$_2$ and the CP radical toward circumstellar shells along with the provided reaction pathway, $c$-C$_3$HCP is a potentially present astro-molecule which could be searched for in phosphorus rich environments. The reaction of CP and benzene (C$_6$H$_6$) to produce phosphaethynyl benzene (C$_6$H$_5$CP) is also explored. A marginally emerged, but tentative, transition state is identified for this reaction using certain quantum chemical approaches but not others. Consequently, the formation of CP-substituted benzoid polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) in astrophysical environments from CP + PAH reactions is possible but currently uncertain. Additionally, explicitly correlated coupled cluster quartic force field and second-order vibrational perturbation theory rovibrational analysis of the vibrational frequencies and rotational constants of $c$-C$_3$HCP are provided, as well as density functional theory predictions of the same for CP-benzene (C$_6$H$_5$CP) and both isomers of CP-naphthalene (C$_1$$_0$H$_7$CP). Our results suggest that IR searches for these molecules would likely be unsuccessful due to the low intensities and coincidence with PAH features, but their large dipole moments could make them feasible to detect with radio astronomy. The barrierless formation of $c$-C$_3$HCP and possibly barrierless synthesis of C$_6$H$_5$CP stand as examples for future investigations of other CP-substituted aromatic molecules, marking the potential beginning of a new frontier of astronomical aromatic functionalization.

title: Rest-frame Ultraviolet Variability of Quasars in the Cosmic Himalayas Overdensity
summary: Some high-redshift overdensities show an enhanced incidence of AGNs, suggesting that large-scale environment may influence supermassive black hole fuelling and triggering. Whether environment also affects AGN variability remains this http URL the Cosmic Himalayas (CH), an extreme concentration of 11 type 1 quasars at z=2.16-2.20, we investigate possible offsets in rest-frame ultraviolet variability relative to quasars with comparable redshifts, black hole masses, and Eddington this http URL construct a parent sample of 1,138 Stripe 82 quasars at 2.11<=z<=2.25 and combine photometry from the SDSS, the PS1, and the ZTF to build observer-frame g- and r-band light curves spanning up to 27~yr. We compare DRW parameters and ensemble structure functions (SFs) with control pseudo-samples matched in black hole mass and Eddington ratio, and use injection--recovery simulations to forecast the detectability of a CH-like this http URL CH quasars show a tendency toward shorter DRW damping timescales (median offsets of -0.32 and -0.13 dex in g and r) and slightly higher asymptotic amplitudes. None of the four DRW comparisons is statistically significant, including the largest offset in the g-band damping timescale (p=0.16). Ensemble SFs generally exceed matched-control medians, although 18 of 19 lag bins per band remain within the 95% pointwise envelopes. Assuming a true uniform -0.32 dex g-band timescale offset, injection--recovery simulations predict an 80% probability of nominal 3sigma detection with approximately 60 quasars of comparable variability scatter and data this http URL confirmed, the tentative variability offsets may suggest that large-scale environment influences accretion-flow variability beyond its potential role in quasar triggering. Larger samples with higher-precision light curves, such as those expected from the LSST, are required to test this possibility.

title: The Milky Way's Early Disk Was Built in Bursts. II. The Multi-component Age-Metallicity Structure of the High-$α$ Disk
comment: 19 pages, 13 figures, Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Whether the high-$\alpha$ disk experienced a continuous or episodic star-formation history remains an open question. Here we investigate the age--metallicity distribution of the high-$\alpha$ disk using approximately 145,000 Gaia DR3 subgiants with $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]>-1$, 6.5~kpc $\lesssim R\lesssim9.5$~kpc, and $|Z|\lesssim1.5$~kpc. We adopt a forward-modelling framework that accounts for individual age and metallicity uncertainties and corrects for sample selection effects. The reconstructed distribution reveals two components: a broad, dominant population peaking at $\sim10.6$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.38$, and an older, more metal-poor population peaking at $\sim12.4$ Gyr and $[\mathrm{Fe/H}]\simeq-0.79$. These features suggest an episodic history of star formation and chemical enrichment in the high-$\alpha$ disk, qualitatively consistent with cosmological simulations in which recurrent gas accretion drives variations in the star formation rate. The age of the older component is close to the $\sim12.3$~Gyr epoch inferred for the proposed Low-energy--Kraken--Heracles accretion event, suggesting a possible connection between this early interaction and enhanced disk star formation. There is tentative evidence that the dominant population is possibly composed of two sub-components with age distributions peaking at $\sim11.1$ Gyr and $\sim10.0$ Gyr, respectively. Together, these results favour a picture in which the high-$\alpha$ disk was built through recurrent episodes of enhanced star formation rather than a single temporally smooth phase, even for the regime of ${\rm [Fe/H]}>-1$.

title: A 13 Year Black Hole Microlensing Survey in Omega Centauri
comment: 17 pages, 17 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Star clusters are born with massive stars that leave behind a large population of stellar mass black holes. These black holes may account for a large fraction of binary black hole mergers seen in gravitational waves as the dense environment enables retention of black holes and the formation of binaries. However, direct measurements of stellar mass black holes in globular clusters are limited, with just a few found in binary systems thus far. In this paper, we examine the possibility of detecting black holes through microlensing in the Milky Way's most massive star cluster, Omega Centauri. We take advantage of a unique dataset of nearly 200 single-band images taken over 13 years with the Hubble Space Telescope to look for the $\sim$1 year long events expected from microlensing of cluster stars by stellar mass black holes. We develop a novel cost function to fit the lensing signatures that we verify using synthetic events, quantifying our completeness. These synthetic events are based on a recent Monte Carlo simulation of Omega Centauri. We also use these synthetic events to train a neural network to most efficiently distinguish observed lensing events. Application of this algorithm to our observed data, and subsequent visual follow-up, show no convincing candidate black hole lensing events. Based on analysis of the simulation data and our completeness, we find that no events would be expected in the data contrary to the expectations from earlier work. We release the photometric dataset used in this work for future use.

title: Lomb-Scargle Recovery of Periodic Binary Signals across Black Hole Mass and Cadence
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables
summary: Searches for periodic supermassive black hole binaries in quasar light curves rely on recovery fractions, the share of injected signals detected, which forecasts use as detection efficiencies. Lin, Charisi, & Haiman (2026) measured them for the Lomb-Scargle periodogram on damped-random-walk light curves matched to 12,400 bright, high-mass Palomar Transient Factory (PTF) quasars with Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 (DR7) masses. To test them over four decades of mass, we inject their sinusoidal and sawtooth signals into light curves of mergers in the TNG100-1 cosmological simulation, with magnitudes drawn from DR7 quasars of similar mass (extrapolated at low mass). We apply their threshold in each frequency bin, set by $10^5$ noise-only light curves per binary, on observed PTF cadences, one Stripe 82 cadence and an LSST-like cadence (Legacy Survey of Space and Time). At fixed absolute magnitude $M_i=-23$, sinusoid recovery falls toward high mass, and with DR7 magnitudes it climbs above about $10^8\,M_\odot$, so the magnitude assignment sets the sign of the trend. Above $10^8\,M_\odot$, where their sample lies, PTF sinusoid recovery is 39.8 against their 44.7 per cent. At LSST-like cadence sinusoid recovery is 76.9 per cent, about three times their 22.6 per cent, for reasons mostly unidentified. Denser sampling of the same PTF baselines did not lower recovery in any test. Even at LSST-like cadence we miss most sawtooth signals above $10^8\,M_\odot$. We tabulate recovery per 0.5-dex mass bin and cadence, with low-mass values likely too high for a deeper survey.

title: A recurring changing state AGN discovered in the SAMI Galaxy Survey and SDSS
comment: 12 pages, 5 figures. Accepted for publication in PASA
summary: We present a detailed analysis of the AGN in galaxy J085337.26+014303.6 at z=0.0582. A combination of SDSS and SAMI Galaxy Survey data shows that this object has gone through at least one full changing-look AGN cycle, from type 1.9 in 2001 to type 1 in 2015 and 2021, and then type 1.9 again in 2022. While the broad lines in this object show evidence of dust obscuration, detailed spectral analysis plus WISE photometry demonstrate that the changes in this object are related to a physical state change, not changing obscuration. In fact, the WISE light curve suggests that this object may have briefly returned to a type 1.9 state in 2020. In the optical, the host galaxy dominates the light (e.g. only ~10 per cent contribution from the AGN at 4000 Angstoms within a central aperture), even in the high state. In contrast, the brightest WISE W2-band measurements place the AGN at a similar luminosity to the entire host galaxy. The broad Balmer lines show evidence of multiple components, with a weak very-broad component (FWHM=5000-6000 km/s) visible in the low type 1.9 state, and a stronger broad component of FWHM~2000 km/s dominating in the high type 1 state. We propose that this is caused by two spatially distinct regions within the broad line region.

title: Discovering supernovae in the Virgo Cluster during the LSST era
comment: submitted to ApJ -- comments welcome
summary: In the era of unprecedentedly wide, deep and high-cadence sky surveys the chance for discovering new explosive transients in nearby, rich galaxy clusters within hours after explosion is expected to increase dramatically. In this paper we focus on the Virgo cluster ($D \simeq 16.5$ Mpc), and estimate the expected numbers of new, very young supernovae in different sub-structures and galaxy types of the cluster during the proposed lifetime (~10 years) of the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) by the Vera Rubin Observatory. These predictions will be tested observationally during the ongoing Shadow-LSST discovery and follow-up program led by University of Arizona in the upcoming years.

title: A neural-network model to find correlations in astrochemical space
comment: Accepted for publication in Astronomy and Astrophysics
summary: The detection of new interstellar molecules is central to astrochemistry, and arguably the most transformative development in the field in past decade has been the increase in both number and diversity of detected species. Using natural language processing models, we develop a machine-learning pipeline, similar to other approaches reported in the literature, to connect molecular structures, encoded as chemical strings, and molecular column densities in TMC-1. The workflow generates astrochemically informed embeddings that can be employed in subsequent supervised learning tasks. These representations are used within a neural-network framework to perform column-density regression on both the original molecular inventory and out-of-distribution species. The resulting model achieves mean squared error values of 0.17/0.58 and mean absolute error values of 0.29/0.59, and coefficients of determination of 0.88/0.51 for the train+validation and validation datasets. The latent vectors learned by the model are rich mathematical objects that capture the underlying chemical relations and also the potential interstellar detectability of the molecule. Using these vectors in molecules obtained from systematic permutations of the TMC-1 inventory, we identify several promising candidates for future detection in this cloud, together with a large number of apolar species. By training the model on datasets reflecting different historical epochs of molecular detections in TMC-1, we show that recent molecular detections have substantially reshaped our understanding of interstellar chemistry, in a transformative, rather than incremental, way. Beyond accurate prediction of column-density trends for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution molecules, the latent-space representations produced by the model provide a stepping stone for developing new forms of data-driven astrochemical intuition and exploration.

title: Stability of rotation axis of galactic disks in HESTIA suite
comment: 8 pages, 4 figures
summary: We have found that in approximately 1/4 of Milky Way or M31 analogues in the HESTIA suite of simulations there is a significant, $>45^\circ$, change in the axis of rotation orientation of the gaseous disk during the last 6 Gyr. In 6 out of 7 such cases the change is likely caused by the accretion of individual satellites, while in one case such a connection is not obvious. All galaxies that underwent a significant change in rotation axis direction also had angular momentum amplitudes below the sample median 6 Gyr ago. Our findings support the idea that last 6~Gyr was a quiet phase of evolution in the LG. On the other hand, the mechanism we detect, that satellites can flip galaxy orientation, can explain the difficulties in identifying correlations between the rotation axis and the orientation of large-scale structure elements.

title: EP J062132.0+623837: A Multi-wavelength Study of a Changing-look Active Galactic Nucleus Discovered by Einstein Probe
comment: 16 pages, 9 figures, 2 tables. Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: EP J062132.0+623837 is a new X-ray source identified in 14-day binned survey data from the Wide-field X-ray Telescope aboard the Einstein Probe (EP). Subsequent X-ray observations with the Follow-up X-ray Telescope (FXT) on board EP localized the source to the central region of the galaxy 2MASX J06213207+6238390 at $z=0.084$. Here, we present a comprehensive analysis of the multi-wavelength data for this object. During the FXT and Swift/XRT follow-up, the source remained X-ray active, with observed luminosities of $(3-9)\times10^{43}$ erg s$^{-1}$, and its X-ray spectra were well described by power-law models with photon indices of $\Gamma\sim1.5$. The optical spectrum of the host galaxy clearly reveals a broad-line active galactic nucleus (AGN) exhibiting significantly enhanced broad Balmer emission lines compared to an archival spectrum obtained four years earlier, thereby marking a changing-look transition from Type 1.8 to Type 1.5. Furthermore, long-term optical and mid-infrared light curves indicate that the nucleus underwent dramatic brightening around 2010 and has since shown substantial variability. Given the spatial coincidence and multi-wavelength behavior, we identify EP J062132.0+623837 as a changing-look AGN, initially detected by EP and subsequently confirmed to exhibit large-amplitude variability across multiple bands. This case study demonstrates the great potential of wide-field time-domain X-ray surveys for discovering changing-look AGNs, paving a new avenue for their systematic identification as a powerful complement to ongoing optical surveys.

title: Self-Supervised Representation Learning for JWST Galaxy Images and Low Resolution Spectra
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for the NeurIPS 2026 RPS Workshop. Comments welcome. Detailed descriptions of the data, model training and additional benchmarks are included in the appendix (11 pages, 4 figures)
summary: A self-supervised multimodal model recovers galaxy stellar masses from sparse JWST data that lack the multi-band coverage required by traditional SED fitting. We train on single-band F150W imaging paired with observed-frame 1-2 $\mu$m PRISM spectra and obtain a joint image-spectrum representation that recovers stellar mass at $1<z\le3$ with $R^2 \sim 0.9$ and $\sigma_{\mathrm{NMAD}} = 0.24$ dex; cross-modal CLIP alignment further raises single-modality performance by $\Delta R^2 = +0.04$ (imaging) and $+0.09$ (spectroscopy), narrowing the gap to joint-modality inference. The code and documentation are available at \href{ this https URL }{GitHub}.

title: A Catalog of Spectral Properties for DESI DR1 Quasars
comment: 17 pages, 10 figures, and 2 tables. Preprint version; comments and feedback are welcome
summary: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) is carrying out a five-year spectroscopic survey designed to map the large-scale structure of the Universe and obtain spectra for millions of galaxies and quasars over a wide redshift range. We present a value-added catalog of spectral properties for 1,717,774 unique quasars (1,774,723 spectra) in the DESI Data Release 1. We perform a uniform spectral decomposition of the quasar continuum, host galaxy emission (at $z<1$), and \FeII\ emission, and measure the line properties of major broad and narrow emission lines from Ly$\alpha$ to H$\alpha$ covered by DESI spectra. We also provide single-epoch black hole mass estimates (from H$\beta$, \MgII, and \CIV), bolometric luminosities, and Eddington ratios for these quasars. We provide systemic redshifts that account for the intrinsic velocity shifts of individual lines; they agree with the DESI pipeline redshifts to within 500~km s$^{-1}$ for 88.6\% of the sample, and are most useful at $z>1$ where the pipeline redshift is heavily constrained by blueshifted high-ionization lines. We also provide local fits to several optical coronal lines, including \NeV~$\lambda3426$, [\ion{Fe}{7}]~$\lambda5722$, [\ion{Fe}{7}]~$\lambda6088$, and [\ion{Fe}{11}]~$\lambda7893$. We show that several emission-line ratios, including those involving coronal lines, vary systematically with Eddington ratio. The catalog is intended as a community resource for studies of quasar demographics, black hole accretion, emission-line physics, and the connection between the broad-, coronal-, and narrow-line regions.

title: SpecLess: A Multi Survey Python Package for Machine Learning Classification of Galaxy Morphology and Activity from Photometry
comment: 14 pages, 2 figures, 15 tables. Submitted to Astronomy & Computing. SpecLess v0.3.0. Open source Python package available at this https URL
summary: Broad band photometry enables scalable galaxy classification without spectroscopy at inference time, yet strong within survey performance may not transfer when the same galaxies are measured by another survey. We present SpecLess, an open source Python package implementing two photometric classification tasks: high confidence Galaxy Zoo 1 elliptical and spiral morphologies, and four SDSS spectroscopic activity reference classes (starforming, starburst, Seyfert, and LINER). Using SDSS+AllWISE, KiDS+VIKING, and DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys photometry, survey specific XGBoost classifiers achieve held out macro F1 scores of 0.9332 (SDSS; 35,554 galaxies) and 0.9237 (KiDS; 3,269) for morphology, and 0.7637 (SDSS; 16,931) and 0.7398 (DESI; 11,975) for activity. Starforming and starburst references are recovered more effectively than Seyfert and LINER, while feature ablations reveal complementary contributions from optical and mid infrared photometry. We quantify catalogue dependence using separately trained common feature models evaluated on matched galaxies with identical labels and data partitions. Relative to target trained models, macro F1 deficits are 0.0153 (SDSS to KiDS) and 0.0354 (KiDS to SDSS) for morphology (12,301 galaxies; 20 splits), and 0.0660 (SDSS to DESI) and 0.0406 (DESI to SDSS) for activity (11,975 test galaxies). Colour only refits, additive corrections, and optical infrared substitutions reveal direction dependent sensitivity without consistently recovering target trained performance. SpecLess v0.3.0 distributes four pretrained, survey specific classifiers through a unified Python interface. The package provides a reproducible baseline for photometric galaxy classification across multiple surveys while establishing an extensible, open source foundation for future developments in classification methods and photometric catalogue support.

title: Odd radio circle J1555+2726: Observational evidence for shock re-acceleration of fossil plasma
comment: 11 pages (+3 pages appendix). Resubmitted to A&A after referee's report
summary: Context. Odd radio circles (ORCs) are peculiar extragalactic sources recently discovered. They are characterised by one or more bright rings extending on scales of hundreds of kiloparsecs, and are filled with fainter emission. A massive elliptical galaxy lies at the centre of ORCs. While their formation mechanism is debated, a shock is plausibly involved. Aims. We aim to constrain the nature of ORC J1555+2726 (ORC4) through the analysis of its morphological and spectral properties. Methods. We utilised Low Frequency ARray (LOFAR), upgraded Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope (uGMRT), and MeerKAT radio data at 50-1284 MHz to obtain images and spectral index maps at high resolution and sensitivity. Results. Both the resolution and observing frequency affect the observed morphology. In particular, the brightness contrast between the ring and the filling emission becomes progressively smoother from higher to lower frequencies. We measured an integrated spectrum of slope $\alpha=1.06\pm 0.03$, a radio power of $P_{\rm 150}= (5.4\pm 0.5)\times 10^{25} \; {\rm W \; Hz^{-1}}$ at 150 MHz, and a radial spectral flattening down to $\alpha\sim0.5$ at the ring location. However, we inferred a negative (convex) spectral curvature and a peculiar spectral shape in radio colour-colour diagrams, which imply spectral flattening towards high frequencies. These properties cannot be explained by shock acceleration of thermal particles and standard ageing. Conclusions. The observed features suggest that a mixture of electrons with different spectra coexist within ORC4 volume, likely associated with shock re-acceleration of a fossil relativistic reservoir. The ring emission is plausibly dominated by higher-energy electrons re-accelerated at the shock front, while lower-energy re-accelerated electrons are more uniformly distributed across the whole source (possibly ellipsoidal) volume.

title: SIGNN++: Robust Graph Neural Star Identification on Earth
comment: 9 pages, 9 figures, 4 tables
summary: We present SIGNN++, a learning-based star identification (SID) framework for celestial navigation in GNSS-denied nighttime environments. Although researchers have developed learning-based SID methods to improve robustness to observation noise, prior evaluations have focused mainly on synthetic or non-terrestrial environments, leaving their reliability under real terrestrial conditions unclear. To address these limitations, SIGNN++ extends SIGNN, a graph neural network-based SID method, with three components: a more realistic noise model for training data, Fourier Transform (FT) of angular-distance edge features, and RANSAC-based Perspective Star Alignment for identification and attitude refinement. The results show that SIGNN++ is more robust to terrestrial observation disturbances and achieves higher star identification accuracy and solved rates than the original SIGNN and publicly available SID baselines, while maintaining comparable attitude accuracy and practical computation time for continuous operation. The implementation code of SIGNN++ and datasets will be available at this https URL .

title: Astro2Method: Benchmarking LLMs on Machine Learning Method Selection in Astronomy
comment: 15 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables
summary: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used in astronomy, but choosing a suitable method for a scientific problem often requires expertise in both astronomy and ML. Large language models (LLMs) could help astronomers make such choices, yet this ability remains underexplored in existing benchmarks. We introduce Astro2Method, a benchmark of 500 expert-reviewed binary questions from 346 astronomy papers (2024/01-2026/06), based on clear performance differences and complete (Easy) or partial (Hard) explanations from the authors. Across five LLMs, direct prompting achieves 87.50-92.55% accuracy on Easy questions but only 58.87-64.52% on Hard. Using historical papers, neither retrieval-augmented generation nor most agent methods with additional reasoning or retrieval (including ReAct, Self-Ask, and CRITIC) bring consistent improvement. Agents required to search the web improve accuracy mainly when they find the papers the questions are based on, with no consistent improvement otherwise. Providing the source paper's pipeline description with method names masked improves Hard accuracy, matching or exceeding web search. Together, these results suggest that relevant experimental information helps distinguish ML methods, but inferring it from related studies and domain knowledge remains challenging for LLMs in astronomy.

title: A Technical Reanalysis of the Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release Experiment
comment: 23 pages, 2 figures, 1 table. Submitted to Astrobiology
summary: The 1976 Viking Carbon Assimilation-Pyrolytic Release (CAPyR) experiment tested whether carbon from $^{14}$CO$_2$ and $^{14}$CO entered Martian soil during a 120-hour incubation in a form retained during a 120 $^\circ$C purge but released by pyrolysis at 635 $^\circ$C. Untrapped radioactivity was measured as Peak 1; material retained in an organic vapor trap was oxidized and measured as Peak 2. Net Peak 2 was intended to represent synthesized reduced organic carbon. Seven of nine usable incubations at Chryse and Utopia Planitia yielded significant net Peak 2 signals, including the dark U1 run. An underreported Viking Lander 2 gas leak introduces uncertainty into U1-U3. The C1 signal corresponds to approximately 10 or 30 pmol of carbon, assuming derivation entirely from CO or CO$_2$, respectively. We reassess these results in light of the possible presence of perchlorate salts in Viking soils. Oxidation of fixed organic radiocarbon during pyrolysis could have shifted label from Peak 2 to Peak 1, a perchlorate-specific effect not considered in previous CAPyR analyses. Hubbard's (1979) mineral-substrate experiments produced abiotic Peak 2 signals without reproducing the heat sensitivity. No demonstrated abiotic mechanism has reproduced all CAPyR observations under Mars-relevant conditions. The observations remain consistent with a biological carbon-assimilation system whose relevant activity survives C5's 120 $^\circ$C/90 $^\circ$C pretreatment but is strongly impaired by C2's 175 $^\circ$C pretreatment. Together with the Labeled Release experiment, CAPyR suggests oxidative and reductive chemistry in separate aliquots from common Martian soil acquisitions. Metabolically active life combines these processes; a quantitative abiotic explanation of their combined heat-labile response patterns remains to be demonstrated.

title: The Pandora SmallSat: post-launch operations and mission update
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures; paper published as proceedings of the SPIE
summary: The Pandora SmallSat is a NASA flight project designed to study the atmospheres of exoplanets. Transmission spectroscopy of transiting exoplanets provides our best opportunity to identify the makeup of planetary atmospheres in the coming decade, and is a key science driver for HST and JWST. Stellar photospheric inhomogeneity due to star spots, however, has been shown to contaminate the observed spectra in these high-precision measurements. Pandora will address the problem of stellar contamination by collecting long-duration photometric observations sampled over a stellar rotation period with a visible-light channel and simultaneous spectra with a near-IR channel. These simultaneous multiwavelength observations will constrain star spot covering fractions of exoplanet host stars, enabling star and planet signals to be disentangled in transmission spectra to then reliably determine exoplanet atmosphere compositions. Pandora will observe exoplanets with sizes ranging from Earth-size to Jupiter-size and host stars spanning mid-K to late-M spectral types. Pandora was selected in early 2021 as part of NASA's inaugural Astrophysics Pioneers Program. Herein, we present an overview of the mission, including the science objectives, operations, the observatory, science planning, and upcoming milestones as we prepare for launch readiness in 2025.

title: Photometric classification and out-of-taxonomy detection of ZTF transients with FLARE
comment: 21 pages, 10 figures
summary: Photometric classifiers decide which of the million nightly alerts of time-domain surveys receive one of the few thousand spectra taken each year, and they are the first place where a transient outside the trained classes can be noticed. We present flare, the photometric classification and anomaly-detection module of AppleCiDEr, evaluated on 10 497 spectroscopically confirmed ZTF transients in six classes and 53 objects from families outside the taxonomy. Catalogue context raises the macro F1 score, with the largest gains where the defining information is absent from the light curve. Blind detection recovers few out-of-taxonomy objects at a 1% false-alarm rate, while a simulated review loop recovers 83% of them after inspecting 15% of the stream. The first confirmations of a new family are most useful in the feature space: with the same eleven labels, a head on the frozen features detects 68% of the tidal disruption events hidden from the training against 57% for a combiner over the anomaly scores, and retraining with them as a new class reaches 85%. The module runs in production on Fritz, the ZTF instance of SkyPortal, and its alarm is reported as a false-alarm rate per unit time on the stream, calibrated on the photometry that the service receives

title: Astrometric detection of rocky exoplanets from inexpensive space platforms
comment: In Proc. SPIE 14145, Space Telescopes and Instrumentation 2026: Optical, Infrared, and Millimeter Wave, 1414510 (21 Aug 2026)
summary: The detection of orbiting exoplanets by way of astrometric monitoring of the host star to reveal gravitationally induced reflex motion requires extreme precision and measurement stability when targeting Earth-mass objects. Despite this, astrometry is widely regarded as the most promising avenue for the most desired of all targets: true Earth analogue systems in the solar neighbourhood. Formerly thought to require flagship class investment, recently several smaller concepts such as the TOLIMAN and SHERA missions have shown that detections are possible, at least in principle, from more modest space platforms. A key enabling feature is that these missions exploit narrow-angle astrometry. Observing only multiple star systems where the target provides its own astrometric reference greatly alleviates the challenges confronted by traditional astrometry with its reliance on distant, faint field stars. This principle underlies the TOLIMAN mission, for which progress and status is reported. However, only a tiny handful of nearby star systems are suited to such a TOLIMAN-like architecture. This paper discusses speculative optical concepts featuring ultra-stable telescopes of modest (<0.5m) aperture designed for astrometric monitoring of isolated single stars at the micro-arcsecond scales required for the discovery of Earth mass objects orbiting sun-like stars in temperate orbits. In simulation, highly sought-after neighbourhood systems such as Epsilon Eridani and Tau Ceti can be exhaustively searched for rocky planets with dedicated observing campaigns spanning several years, all from relatively inexpensive orbital platforms.

title: Science-driven design and performance evaluation of a Silicon Laue Component lens for hard X-ray polarimetry
comment: 6 pages. 2 figures. Submitted to Astronomy & Astrophysics
summary: Focusing hard X-rays above 80 keV is challenging for grazing-incidence optics. Laue lenses offer an alternative based on crystal diffraction. We assess a lens based on Silicon Laue Components (SiLCs), consisting of stacked silicon plates, for polarimetry of accreting stellar-mass black holes and strongly magnetized neutron stars in the 80-200 keV band. We derive effective-area requirements from the minimum detectable polarization at 99% confidence (MDP99) for an XL-Calibur-inspired polarimeter observing a 100-mCrab source for 100 ks. We evaluate an 18-m-focal-length lens combining Si(220) and Si(111) reflections, with a 63 arcsec diffraction bandpass and a 90% optical filling factor, using on-axis ray tracing of a perfectly aligned lens with uniform crystal curvatures. An MDP99 of 5% requires mean effective areas of approximately 260, 400, and 740 cm^2 in the 80-100, 100-130, and 130-200 keV bands, respectively. The lens spans radii of 356-1453 mm and continuously covers 80-200 keV. Its effective area reaches approximately 375 cm^2 near the low-energy boundary and falls to approximately 200 cm^2 at 180 keV. The focal-plane diameters enclosing 50% and 90% of the focused signal are 5.4 mm (62 arcsec) and 9.8 mm (112 arcsec). Mean effective areas of approximately 320, 250, and 220 cm^2 give reference MDP99 values of approximately 4.5%, 6.4%, and 9.5% in the three bands. The design reaches few-percent polarimetric sensitivity below 100 keV but does not maintain a 5% MDP99 across 80-200 keV under the adopted detector assumptions. It remains relevant for more strongly polarized hard components and provides a reference for end-to-end optimization of the optics, detector response, and background.

title: Simulation-based inference of profile evolution for high-precision pulsar timing
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Pulsars are exceptional cosmic laboratories, the most stable of which rival atomic clocks. Nearly all of that precision rests on one observable, the average pulse profile unique to each pulsar and stable over decades. These profiles change shape systematically with observing frequency, reflecting the physics of the emitting pulsar beam, but if left unmodelled, it can bias the arrival-time measurements, undermining precision timing. Profile-domain timing has been proposed to address this effect, but current implementations use stochastic sampling, which is computationally prohibitive and has limited the application in large-scale analyses. Here, we present a simulation-based inference approach to profile-domain timing, using a normalising flow conditioned on a convolutional embedding of the frequency-phase portrait. From a single portrait, it returns joint posteriors on dispersion measures, arrival times, and the parameters governing profile evolution instantaneously, with uncertainties verified against known inputs following an initial training run. The value of a likelihood-free approach is that the simulator becomes the interface to pulsar properties. Fundamental properties like non-Gaussian noise, pulsar self-noise, jitter, scattering, and profile change can be inferred by simulating them rather than by deriving a new likelihood for each, opening a promising pathway to include machine learning methods into pulsar timing workflows.

title: A Generalized Framework for Rapid Polarization Response Generation in Wide Field-of-View Compton Polarimeters
comment: 34 pages, 18 figures, Accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: Polarimetry is the most direct probe of the unsettled radiation mechanism and magnetic field structure of gamma-ray burst (GRB) prompt emission at the energies where it peaks, tens of keV to about 1 MeV. Compton polarimeters use the azimuthal scattering angle distribution (ASAD), a 180 degree modulation on axis. GRB measurements have largely relied on the on-axis modulation factor $\mu_{100}$. For a wide field-of-view planar polarimeter, GRBs arrive off axis, where the Klein-Nishina projection adds harmonics to the ASAD. Muleri (2014) described this projection and evaluated it in a low-energy expansion for X-rays. We evaluate it numerically without approximation over the whole prompt-emission energy band for any incidence and polarization angles, quantify the off-axis harmonics a single modulation factor cannot capture, and verify the model against GEANT4 simulations of an ideal polarimeter. We also include the effect of the detection threshold on the ASAD. With POLAR as the case study, we present two modes that build the full polarization response with at least 95 percent fewer Monte Carlo simulations. Mode 1 takes only the unpolarized simulation per energy and recovers the polarization measured with POLAR's full GEANT4 responses for all but the brightest GRBs, where it underestimates the polarization degree. Mode 2 adds two polarized simulations per energy at distinct angles and reproduces the simulated ASADs to their statistical noise and the polarization of every GRB tested. Both modes are released as open-source software for any planar Compton polarimeter.

title: Lomb-Scargle Recovery of Periodic Binary Signals across Black Hole Mass and Cadence
comment: 26 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables
summary: Searches for periodic supermassive black hole binaries in quasar light curves rely on recovery fractions, the share of injected signals detected, which forecasts use as detection efficiencies. Lin, Charisi, & Haiman (2026) measured them for the Lomb-Scargle periodogram on damped-random-walk light curves matched to 12,400 bright, high-mass Palomar Transient Factory (PTF) quasars with Sloan Digital Sky Survey Data Release 7 (DR7) masses. To test them over four decades of mass, we inject their sinusoidal and sawtooth signals into light curves of mergers in the TNG100-1 cosmological simulation, with magnitudes drawn from DR7 quasars of similar mass (extrapolated at low mass). We apply their threshold in each frequency bin, set by $10^5$ noise-only light curves per binary, on observed PTF cadences, one Stripe 82 cadence and an LSST-like cadence (Legacy Survey of Space and Time). At fixed absolute magnitude $M_i=-23$, sinusoid recovery falls toward high mass, and with DR7 magnitudes it climbs above about $10^8\,M_\odot$, so the magnitude assignment sets the sign of the trend. Above $10^8\,M_\odot$, where their sample lies, PTF sinusoid recovery is 39.8 against their 44.7 per cent. At LSST-like cadence sinusoid recovery is 76.9 per cent, about three times their 22.6 per cent, for reasons mostly unidentified. Denser sampling of the same PTF baselines did not lower recovery in any test. Even at LSST-like cadence we miss most sawtooth signals above $10^8\,M_\odot$. We tabulate recovery per 0.5-dex mass bin and cadence, with low-mass values likely too high for a deeper survey.
